To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) prisoner autobiographies are a valuable resource for teaching probation officers; 2) they are a neglected source of knowledge for probation training; 3) they have the potential to develop a preliminary theoretical understanding of desistance; and 4) they can be used as a basis for discussion of what works in probation and penal reform.

probation training can be enhanced by using prisoner autobiographies in a variety of ways, and that this is particularly the case when the training is delivered to a group of probation officers in training.
In summary, our research is concerned with

(a) the use of autobiographical material in probation training; (b) the use of such material as an introduction to the study of desistance; (c) the use of the autobiographical genre as a resource for debate on what works and what doesn't in probation and prison; (d) the use of this material to ground probation training in a distinctive crininalogical discourse, and (e) the use of a particular kind of autobiographical material to open up a debate

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
probation training needs to draw on the life history approach to offender autobiographies in order to develop a preliminary and critical understanding of desistance.

prisoner autobiographies can be usefully deployed to help students develop an understanding of desistance and the process of re-integration into mainstream society, and that they can be used to stimulate a critical discussion on what works and what doesn't in the rehabilitation of offenders.
prisoner autobiographies are a rich and underused resource in probation training, which can be used to good effect to develop a critical and constructive understanding of desistance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of prisoner autobiographies in probation training can: (1) help probation officers to understand the process of desistance from crime and the importance of social capital in this; (2) provide a basis for debate on what works in the rehabilitation of offenders and what doesn’t; and (3) provide a basis from which probation officers can develop an understanding of how penal reform has developed in Britain and how they can contribute to it.

the autobiographical genre is a rich and underused source for probation training and that, in the case of prisoner autobiographies, the best of this genre has been and continues to be a major resource for penal reform.
the autobiographies of offenders and prisoners, and the life history approach more generally, have much to offer the probation curriculum.
The main takeaway from our work is that
probation training should be more open to, and critical of, the criminological tradition which has produced the autobiographies discussed.
the life story approach to offender auto/biographies can be a useful way to begin a training programme for probation officers.

the use of prisoner auto/biographies in training can be an important means of engaging trainees in debate on the effectiveness of the probation service in the light of its current and future role in the penal system.
